THE WINDING
from Act One of a play

[The works room of the Marnhill town clock, reached by ninety-one stairs. A drum of cable, a weight shaft going down through the floor, an iron crank leaning in the corner. Late afternoon; the light comes through one small window at the level of the dial. ORSOLA VESK, seventy-four, sits on an upturned crate with her coat still on. DEV ARMITAGE, twenty-six, stands in the doorway holding a folder.]

DEV. The council said four o'clock.

ORSOLA. The council says a good many things up here that it has never come up to check. [She does not get up.] Shut the door, or the dust comes off the stair.

[DEV shuts the door. The room is suddenly quieter; the escapement can be heard, a slow double knock.]

DEV. They have given me a procedure. [He opens the folder.] Eight pages.

ORSOLA. Read me the first line of it.

DEV. "Insert the crank fully before applying any turning force."

ORSOLA. Good. That one is true. [beat] The other seven pages were written by a man who came up once, in June, in dry weather.

DEV. You could have written them.

ORSOLA. I was not asked. [She stands, slowly, and takes up the crank. She does not fit it yet; she holds it out flat on her palms.] Forty-one years, and I have never once wound it on a Friday without thinking the cable would go. It never has. That is not the same as safe.

DEV. How many turns?

ORSOLA. The book will tell you ninety.

DEV. And you?

ORSOLA. Eighty-six, and then you listen. [She fits the crank and gives it one turn. The drum takes it with a hard click.] Four turns is a quarter of an hour of running. I would rather climb up an hour early on a Tuesday than put the last four in and find out what the top of the drum is like this year.

[She steps back and offers him the crank. He takes it. Both their hands are on it for a moment; neither lets go.]

ORSOLA. It will be heavier than you expect at the eighth turn. Everybody's arm believes the weight is at the bottom of the shaft. It is on the drum, on the part you cannot see.

DEV. [winding, counting under his breath] Six. Seven. Eight. — Oh.

ORSOLA. There.

DEV. Nobody put that in the folder.

ORSOLA. No. [She sits back down on the crate and watches him work.] They put in what can be written. What is left over is what I am for, and they have given me until Thursday to hand it across.

[DEV goes on winding. ORSOLA does not count aloud with him, but her hand moves slightly on her knee at each turn.]

explanation: Orsola divides the job in her last speech — "They put in what can be written. What is left over is what I am for" — and the scene is made of that leftover: eighty-six turns instead of ninety, the load sitting "on the part you cannot see," the eighth turn that Dev meets without warning from the pages. That is "what the winder knows that the folder does not." prompt: The narrator's telling is chiefly concerned with what the village does about
passage:
THE THIRD WEIGHT
a tale as it is told in the salt villages of the Dolnik

They tell it this way in Dolnik, and they tell it otherwise one valley over, and I will give you the Dolnik telling because it is the one I was told.

When the salt road still ran, every cart that came down from the pans was weighed at the bridge, and the weigher took one part in twenty for the count's granary. The weigher in this telling is a woman named Zoya, who held the office nine years and was, by every account, honest — which in Dolnik is not a compliment but a description, the way one says that a roof is tin.

One spring the count sent down a new set of weights, cast in the city, with a letter saying the old ones had worn light and had been cheating him. Zoya set the new weights on the bar. Every cart that crossed that week paid more, and the carters said what carters say. But the third weight, the one brought out only for the heaviest loads, rang wrong when it was set down. A sound weight gives a dull sound. This one sang like a cup.

Zoya accused nobody. She carried the third weight to the smith, and the smith opened it, and inside it was hollow to the depth of a thumb, and the hollow was packed with wax and grit — an old trick and not a clever one. Anyone might have done it: the founder in the city, the carrier, the count's own clerk, or Zoya herself, who had had the weight in her house a night.

Here the tellings part. In Dolnik we say she carried the opened weight to the count and laid it on his table and said nothing at all, and that the count, who was no fool, understood that she could have mended it quietly and had chosen not to, and that this was the whole of her cleverness. One valley over they say she never went, and that the smith's wife carried the story instead, and that Zoya was turned out of the office within the year for a thing she had not done.

I do not know which is true. But I will say what my grandmother said when I asked her the same question at the same age. She said the tale is not about the weight. It is about the night the weight spent in Zoya's house, and what Zoya did not do with it, and that a village which keeps two endings for a story has already admitted it cannot answer that, and would rather hold the question than take a liar's certainty.
explanation: The last paragraph says what the two endings are for: the village "has already admitted it cannot answer that, and would rather hold the question than take a liar's certainty." What is kept, and kept deliberately, is "a question it cannot answer." The trick was detected — the weight rang wrong and the smith opened it — and Zoya is turned out of the office in one of the two tellings, so neither "a trick it cannot detect" nor "a weigher it cannot replace" survives the tale's own events.
